The letter was addressed to her aunt, in a hand Sequoia did not know, and she had read only the first line before her pulse began knocking in her ears. She wondered, briefly, who in the world still wrote to Wenhua at all. Then the ladle struck the pot rim, sharp as a gavel, and Sequoia slid the envelope under the flour tin. Outside, the mesa held the last orange light, and the onions hissed in the pan.

items.passage: "Stand still and they'll forget you're here," Ivy said, working the bellows of the smoker until gray clouds drifted over the hives. Hortense obeyed, as she had obeyed in Ivy's classroom thirty years before. The bees grew sluggish and mild, and Ivy lifted out a heavy frame without a single sting. "Smoke doesn't hurt them," Ivy said. "It only tells them not to worry." Hortense remembered the ginger biscuits Ivy used to slip her after school, always on the afternoons the headmaster called her father in. She had thought them comfort. Now, watching the drowsy bees surrender their honey, she wondered what else had been lifted out of that house while she was busy chewing. Ivy offered her a jar of the honey, and Hortense, after a moment, took it.

items.passage:
Three rules my uncle Dewi kept at the loom:
count every thread, owe no one, trust no rival.
We owed the cooperative in Bologna
more than a winter's linen could repay,
and Nora, at the next loom, wove faster than us both.
He called her the competition. I called her nothing.
But when our warp snapped on the morning of the market,
it was Nora who knotted it, thread across thread,
her weft running sideways through our long, straight lines.
Warp holds still; weft crosses over.
Neither one alone is cloth.
By evening the bolt was finished, and my uncle,
counting, lost his place, and laughed, and counted again.
items.question: In the poem, the warp and weft most likely represent which of the following?
options: How opposing forces can bind together into something stronger
The uncle's strict rules for keeping his accounts in order
The debt that grows heavier as the long winter continues
The rivalry that drives each weaver to work ever faster

items.passage: Havana's outskirts still had a post office with a brass telegraph key bolted to the counter, though no message had passed through it in decades. I had come there as a new teacher, Roshane, to teach Morse code to anyone who wanted to learn, and the only one who came was Valentina, fourteen, arms folded, certain the key was a museum piece. Its knob was worn bright, a shallow dip pressed into it by thumbs I would never meet. On the first day Valentina refused to touch it. On the fifth, she tapped out her own name, badly, and set her thumb exactly in that hollow without noticing. By the end of the month she was correcting my rhythm. When I left, the postmistress asked whether to remove the key at last. Valentina answered before I could, and the key stayed.

options: The uselessness of a machine that no longer sends any messages
A skill handed down through many people, now reaching Valentina
Valentina's stubborn resistance to learning from a stranger
The postmistress's wish to modernize the old post office

items.passage: After the winter my father chipped Wilhelmina's blue serving bowl, he turned it every morning so the broken edge faced the kitchen wall. Wilhelmina ran the boarding house in Bergen and counted her dishes the way other people count money, yet she never seemed to see the chip. I saw it. I was eleven and stubborn and had been told I was wrong about everything that year, so I said nothing, which felt like winning. Each morning I watched him rotate the bowl before Leopoldina, the cook, filled it with porridge, and each morning, after he left, I checked that the edge still faced the wall. Neither of us ever spoke of it. When we moved out in spring, he lifted the bowl last, turned it once more, and set it down exactly as it had been.
items.question: In the text, the chipped bowl most likely represents which of the following?
options: The father's careless habits that annoyed the landlady
The family's poverty during their years at the house
A mistake that father and son silently agree to hide
The son's wish to expose his father's carelessness

items.passage: Cornwall's smallest harbor, so the old tale goes, held one boat that belonged to two people: old Ephraim and the granddaughter who had come to learn his tongue. A merchant named Albert offered gold for the boat, enough to fill both their pockets. Ephraim did not answer. Instead he handed the girl a torn net and taught her the old word for each knot as she mended it: one for the knot that holds, one for the knot that forgives, one for the knot that remembers. All winter she mended and spoke, until the words came to her without thinking. In spring Albert returned with more gold. The girl looked at the net spread across the seawall, every knot with a name, and told him the boat was not for sale. Ephraim only nodded and went down to the water.
items.question: In the text, the mended net most likely represents which of the following?
options: The hard labor that the girl secretly wishes to escape
The wealth that Albert hopes to gain from the harbor
The damage that the old boat has suffered over time
The heritage that binds the girl to Ephraim's language

items.passage: Bogdan, the caretaker of the school gymnasium in Riga, let the two women in after hours, as he had every Thursday since the mother's knees began to fail. The daughter swept the long floor while her mother sat on the lowest bench and wound the climbing ropes, slowly, the way she had done for thirty years. In nine days the daughter would board a plane for Toronto and not come back. Neither of them mentioned it. Instead the mother asked Bogdan to turn off the radio, and when the daughter dropped the broom, the clatter rang out alone in the high room. Her mother did not look up. She was practicing the silence, Bogdan thought, the way the girls on the team once practiced a vault before the real meet. He locked the doors behind them at ten.

items.passage: Although they had not spoken in a month, Imani and Themba both arrived at the kite-maker's yard in Addis Ababa on the morning of the festival, each pretending to have come for something else. The festival contract, the one that would have filled both their ovens all year, had gone to a hotel kitchen across the city after each baker's sample arrived late. Themba said Imani had kept the only van. Imani said Themba had never once been on time. Overhead, the kite-maker's children ran with paper hawks and bright diamonds, and a gust tore one of the diamonds loose. That contract, Themba said quietly, was a kite with no string. They watched the loose diamond rise, wobbling, over the eucalyptus trees until it was only a speck.

a festival honor that only the kite-maker had power to grant.
a minor opportunity hardly worth the bakers' long argument.
a chance that had drifted beyond either baker's control.

items.passage:
Once, in a Galician spring, the river climbed
into the cellar of the old clinic, and Rafael,
the night nurse, waded down with a lantern
to carry up the jars of plum preserve
he had meant as a gift for Esteban in bed seven.
Esteban, who could not lift a spoon by then,
looked at the dripping jar a long time
and pushed it back across the blanket.
Keep it, he said. You saved it. It is yours.
Rafael set it on the sill and understood:
in that room where the water kept rising,
the old man's pride still kept its head above water.
The rain went on all night against the shutters.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “kept its head above water” most nearly suggests that Esteban's pride
options: survived despite his growing weakness and dependence.
made him fear that the flood would reach his room.
turned into anger at Rafael for entering the cellar.
gave him hope of recovering enough to leave the clinic.
